notes.1a: The majority of candidates described two ways of improving the accuracy of the measurement. However, a significant number lost marks through vague and inaccurate statements.
notes.1b: The majority of candidates were able to describe a method of calculating the thickness of a sheet of paper. Weaker candidates gave confused statements such as dividing the number of pages by the thickness of the book.
notes.1c: The majority of candidates scored three or four marks. Common errors were to divide mass by 10, failing to convert grams to kilograms, and the omission or use of an incorrect unit. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2017
notes.2a: Many candidates scored this mark. The most common error was electrical closely followed by potential energy.
notes.2bi: The majority of candidates scored full marks. The most common error was to divide the distance from the pivot by the force.
notes.2bii: Many candidates struggled with this question. Only the most able linked ideas such as chemical energy transferred from the student is stored as gravitational potential energy in the lid of the laptop.
notes.2c: The majority of candidates gave two advantages of the solar panel over the mains electrical supply. Weaker candidates gave vague descriptions for renewal energy sources such as eco-friendly or better for the environment; these did not score.
notes.2d: Many candidates realised that the solar panel would take longer to recharge the battery.
notes.3ai: ,(ii),(iii) The majority of candidates scored these marks.
notes.3aiv: Most candidates were able to calculate the average speed of the car. Weaker candidates attempted to calculate the area under the graph, with little success.
notes.3b: The majority of candidates scored both marks. Weaker candidates described the difference in speed but failed to go on to explain how the graph showed the difference in speed.
notes.4a: Many candidates correctly calculated the force on the road from the tyre. The most common error was to use force = pressure ÷ area.
notes.4b: Many candidates scored marks by referring to collisions between molecules, but only the most able referred to collisions with the walls of the tyre.
notes.5a: The majority of candidates were able to complete the flow chart. A common mistake was to reverse the positions of statements A and F.
notes.5b: Many candidates scored both marks, but a disappointing number gave vague or unclear statements which failed to score.
notes.5c: Candidates found this surprisingly difficult, with many giving vague statements such as “it explains how well it works”.
notes.6a: The majority of candidates scored two or three marks. A surprising number of candidates failed to use the three terms given to label the three diagrams.
notes.6bi: ,(ii) Many candidates scored both marks, but a significant number lost marks through failing to indicate distances accurately.
notes.6c: Many candidates scored both marks. It was pleasing to see most candidates showing a correct refraction at the centre of the lens. Unfortunately there are still some candidates who attempt to complete a ray diagram without the use of a ruler. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2017
notes.7a: The majority of candidates correctly indicated the directions of vibrations. Only a small minority gave directions at right angles to the direction of wave travel.
notes.7b: The majority of candidates scored this mark. The most common errors were water and steel.
notes.7ci: Many candidates gave a suitable value for frequency, but failed to give the correct unit.
notes.7cii: Most candidates gave a correct meaning for ultrasound.
notes.8a: The majority of candidates scored two marks, with lamps correctly connected in parallel, and correct symbols for switches drawn. Very few candidates added variable resistors to the circuit.
notes.8b: The majority of candidates gave good descriptions of the purpose of switch X.
notes.8c: A surprisingly large number of candidates could not identify component Y as a fuse, and even fewer gave adequate descriptions of how the fuse works.
notes.9a: A surprisingly large number of candidates thought that tin would be attracted to the magnet, and that a magnet would have no effect on a bar of unmagnetised iron.
notes.9b: Many candidates gave good descriptions of the differences in magnetic properties of soft iron and steel.
notes.10a: Most candidates gave correct names for the two coils. Only the weakest candidates referred to them as top and bottom coils.
notes.10b: The majority of candidates correctly determined the output voltage of the transformer. These candidates usually started by writing down the transformer equation. Candidates who tried to use some form of cross multiplication met with little success.
notes.11a: Many candidates produced good representations of the magnetic field in and around the coil. Many candidates, however, gave the wrong or contradictory directions of the magnetic field.
notes.11bi: ,(ii) The majority of candidates recognised the electromagnet, and most of these went on to give a correct use of electromagnets.
notes.12a: Many candidates gave clear descriptions of how to identify alpha and beta particles, but a significant number lost marks through vague or unclear statements in their descriptions.
notes.12b: Many candidates scored full marks on this question. Weaker candidates tended to confuse the location of the electron and the neutron, and the charge on the neutron and the proton. There were very few candidates who failed to answer this question, indicating that the time for the paper was adequate. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2017
